Hi, Luiza, I am Mark Ellison, and I coordinate exchange students at the law school here. Before we look at your file, tell me a little about your English.
Sure. I have been studying English since I was seven, but honestly, I learned most of it online, watching American videos.
That is more common than you think. And have you ever studied abroad?
Only for one month, in Scotland, last year. It was short, but it gave me a head start, because now I know what a class in English feels like.
Good. You should know that our exchange program is quite competitive. Every year about two hundred students apply for thirty places.
I know. My brother did the same exchange, and when he applied, the cut-off score for the best universities was above ninety.
The scale has changed since then, but the idea has not. The score is the first requirement, and it only gets you shortlisted. What makes a student stand out is the interview.
Then that is what I want to work on. I read a lot, but when I speak about technical things, I sometimes stumble over the words.
You have time. The deadline is in two years, so if you practice every week, you will keep up with the classes easily.
That is exactly why I started now. And which host universities do law students usually choose?

I read exchange applications for six years, and I want to tell you what the committee actually remembers. It is not your score. By the time you reach the interview, everyone in the room has a good score, so the number stops being interesting. What we remember is whether you could explain, in two minutes, why this university and not another one. The strongest candidates did not have the most impressive track record. They had a clear story. Where they were, how long they had been working on something, and where they wanted to go next. And one more thing, because students always worry about it. Nobody on the committee cared about accent. We cared about whether we had to ask you to repeat yourself. If your sentences are clear, your accent is simply part of who you are.

Good afternoon, and thank you for joining this session so early in your degree. Most students come to us six months before the deadline, and that is too late. The application has three parts. First, the language requirement: every partner university asks for an official test, and since the TOEFL moved to a scale from one to six, the most competitive ones expect an overall band of at least four and a half, sometimes five. Second, your grades from the first two years. And third, a short interview, in English, with two members of the committee. Here is my advice. Take a practice test this semester, not next year, so you know exactly how far you are from the cut-off score. Choose three host universities, not one. And remember that a semester abroad is not a vacation. The reading load in a law school is heavy in any language, and you will need to keep up with it from the first week.
